newsitem.title: USA: EU official warns Boeing on merger.
newsitem.headline: EU official warns Boeing on merger.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said Friday Boeing Co. must drop exclusive sales agreements with airline companies as one of the conditions for a merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp.
In Seattle, Boeing Chief Executive Officer Phil Condit said he was confident his company would work out differences with the EU so the deal could close in August.

Van Miert expressed concern that Boeing now has exclusive provider relationships with Delta Air Lines Inc. and American Airlines. That effectively shuts out sales by Airbus Industrie, the European airline manufacturer.

"I can't see how possibly we can give our authorisation to the merger with such a system in place," Van Miert told Reuters after a speech to the European Institute. "To our mind this is something which should be declared illegal. And I have no doubt that, if needed, we are going to do so in the European Union."
But Van Miert added that the ending of exclusive sales agreements would not be enough, in itself, to win EU approval.
"Now, it would not be good enough to bless the merger, that must be clear as well," he said.
Condit said in Seattle he thought any problems could be solved.
"Fundamentally this is a competitive market," Condit said. "We strive hard to win our competitions and get the right products to our customers. I think that's what competition's about."

During recent speeches in the United States, Van Miert has repeatedly expressed concern about Boeing's domination of the airline market. In one speech he noted that Boeing has a 60 percent market share in Europe.

The EU has authority to turn down the merger and, ultimately, to impose fines on the companies of up to 10 percent of annual gross world sales. A final EU administrative decision must be reached on the merger by the end of July, Van Miert said.

If the decision were to go against the merger, Boeing could appeal to the European Court of Justice. Such cases can take 18 months to two years to adjudicate, during which time the merger could be delayed.
Van Miert said he had informed U.S. Federal Trade Commission Chairman Robert Pitofsky of the EU view during a meeting earlier in the day.
"I informed Chairman Pitofsky about the way we are looking upon it," he said.
The FTC is examining the merger in the United States and it is unclear when it will decide what action, if any, to take. If the FTC decides against the merger, it must go to court and challenge it.
Meanwhile, Van Miert said the EU is continuing an in-depth investigation of the merger.

Van Miert said the EU has already communicated its concerns to Boeing and that by May it will finish its investigation. Then the EU will conduct a private hearing with Boeing, discussing remedies to any difficulties it discovers.
